problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as business analytics struggling with rapidly growing, large, and high-dimensional data, especially in finance and other business settings. It says classical machine learning is not scalable enough for these datasets and that QML may help with financial modelling, risk analysis, portfolio calibration, and fraud identification.
problem_statement_quotes: This paper aims at presenting how QML can solve the increasingly challenging demands of big contributions to large-scale data analysis in business contexts, achieving better performance than orthodox machine learning methods in terms of time and efficacy.

In finance, QML has been used in the portfolio management, and more effectively in pricing models instead of the classical models, as QML gives quicker and often precise results than classical models (Orús et al., 2019).
Perhaps, the most popular area of the use of QML is financial modelling wherein, big data analytics is indispensable in risk analysis, portfolio calibration, and fraud identification.
classical_baseline: The paper treats conventional classical machine learning models as the baseline, including support vector machines, deep neural networks, linear regression, and classical Monte Carlo simulations. It also explicitly contrasts QML with classical models in financial modelling and other business analytics tasks.
classical_baseline_quotes: Conventional models of machine learning have transformed business analytics as it enables firms to mine data for insights regarding the behaviour of consumers, productivity of operations, and dynamics of the market (Jordan & Mitchell, 2015).
classical_difficulty: The paper says classical methods struggle with large, complex, and high-dimensional business data. It describes problems of scalability, slower processing, reduced precision, and exponential growth in time and resource use as feature dimensions increase, especially when real-time decisions are needed.
classical_difficulty_quotes: While these approaches are successful in many applications till this day, they fail to address the large and complex ‘big’ business data which are often measured in millions of variables and may be multidimensional.

Such a process comes with lots of complexity when it comes to speed for processing, accuracy and resource utilization, especially when real time data is subject to decision making (Cerezo et al., 2021; Schuld & Killoran, 2019).

Another disadvantage of the classical machine learning methods is their poor scalability to the high-dimensional data, or, in other words, the problem of dimensionality sparsity. When the number of feature sets increases in a dataset, classical algorithms take time, and resources to train in an exponential manner, which renders inefficiency and inaccuracy (Hastie et al., 2009).

However, these models are not scalable to the large and complex datasets characteristic of today’s data mining tasks. With an ever-rising volume of data, the computational resources available to handle such datasets avertly scales up meaning that forms of estimation become slower and less precise (Goodfellow et al., 2016).
business_stakes: The paper says the stakes include faster and more accurate decision-making, competitive advantage, and lower computational cost. In finance specifically, it mentions risk evaluation, portfolio rebalancing, and financial asset decisions as time-sensitive business activities.
business_stakes_quotes: This paper aims to show how QML holds practical value for business analytics, in terms of time efficiency, potency of the predictions, and effectiveness in decision making.

For instance, in the finance sector, where the timing of risk evaluation and portfolio rebalancing is paramount, QML can add a wealth of value, increase the reliability of forecasts and streamline the rates at which financial models are addressed by the Q-DB (Orús et al., 2019).

Likewise, in operations planning and control especially within the retail an supply chain management, QML can enhance the processing of demand estimation and inventory control and enhance operational efficiency at reduced expense (Verdon et al., 2019).
extraction_notes: Paper is a broad business-analytics/QML article, not a finance-specific methods paper; finance appears as one application area alongside supply chain and retail. Classical Monte Carlo is mentioned only in the results section as a comparator.
